summary: For ages 9–11: ocean animals such as humpback whales and sea turtles make remarkable migrations (thousands of miles) driven by two separable factors — following seasonal food supply and reaching safe breeding/nesting sites. Learners should describe one migration in detail, name both drivers, grasp the scale, and reason from shifting resources to the route and its timing. Core insight: the journey is a timed response to a resource that appears and vanishes with the seasons, combined with a need to breed where young are safest.
misconceptions: 'Animals migrate just because it gets cold/they feel like it' — missing the specific food and breeding drivers.
'The journey is short / they wander randomly' — underestimating the thousands-of-miles scale and the directed, repeated route.
'They feed and breed in the same place' — not grasping the separation that necessitates the journey.
'Migration is effortless' — ignoring the energetic cost and risk that make the food/breeding payoff worth it.
Confusing migration (round-trip, repeated, purposeful) with one-way dispersal or getting lost.

activities.title: Migrate through the year with a humpback whale
steps: Start in cold polar seas and advance the seasons step by step (for example with a season dial or by moving through labelled months).
Watch a productivity/food layer bloom in polar summer — feed and fatten the whale while krill are abundant.
As autumn arrives and the bloom fades, decide what to do: staying means little food while a calf is due; set off and travel thousands of miles to warm tropical breeding grounds to calve, then return.
Track the distance travelled on a distance or energy meter and note how mistiming the departure (lingering too long) costs the whale energy and risks the calf.
Optionally switch to a sea-turtle mode that adds returning to nest on the same beach or stretch of coast where the turtle hatched.
State in your own words why the whale leaves rich feeding water for food-poor tropics, and name each leg's driver.
activities.insight: The migration is not restlessness or seeking comfort — it is chasing food that appears and disappears with the seasons AND reaching a safe place to breed, a round trip forced because food and safe breeding sites are not in the same place at the same time.

activities.title: Explore a migration atlas (descriptive case study)
steps: Open a route map of one species' annual migration with tappable waypoints: feeding ground, open-ocean transit, breeding ground.
At each waypoint, read the season, what the animal is doing (feed / travel / breed), and the cumulative distance travelled.
Toggle a seasonal-productivity overlay to see where and when food blooms along the route.
Describe the migration in detail from start to finish, including both drivers and the total distance.
activities.insight: A single species feeds in one place and breeds in another at different times of year, and the specific destinations (particular feeding grounds, a natal beach) matter — the route is directed and repeated, not random wandering or one-way dispersal.

activities.title: Order the year and estimate the scale (check understanding)
steps: Put the annual migration stages in order (feed in polar summer → travel → breed in tropics → return).
Choose between food and breeding as the driver for each leg of the trip.
Estimate the total distance of the migration (slider or multiple choice) and compare to the real figure.
Consider a 'what if': if the polar seas stayed rich in food all year, would the whale still make the trip, and which leg would it still need?
Explain in one or two sentences WHY the timing of departure follows the seasons.
activities.insight: Both drivers and the scale can be stated independently, and the timing of the journey is tied to seasonal change rather than whim; in this model, even with year-round polar food, a whale due to calve would still need to travel to safe warm waters to give birth, so food alone does not explain the journey.

activities.title: Hear from a scientist who tracks tagged animals (wonder supplement)
steps: Listen to or read a marine biologist recounting one tracked humpback's or turtle's year — where it went and when.
Ask or consider the question 'How do they find their way?' and discuss cues such as sensing magnetic fields.
Keep a note of what the animal was doing at each stage to connect the story back to the food and breeding drivers.
activities.insight: Navigation and tracking add wonder and a human perspective, while the core reasoning stays on why (food + breeding) and how far.

checkQuestion: A humpback whale swims thousands of miles from cold polar seas to warm tropical waters and back every year. A child says 'it goes to the warm place because it doesn't like being cold — like us wanting a holiday in the sun'. Do you think staying comfortable is the real reason? What actually drives a journey that long, and how would the whale know when to set off?
checkAnswer: Comfort isn't the driver. Marine migrations are tied to food and breeding on a seasonal cycle: whales feed in cold, nutrient-rich polar waters in summer where food is abundant, then travel to warm tropical waters to breed and give birth where calves are safer, even though there's little food there. The timing is cued by the seasons (changing day length, temperature, food supply), not by a whim. Sea turtles show the reproduction side too — they return to the very beach where they hatched to lay their eggs.
